subject: Art & Design
title: Anchoring Bias: The First Number Wins
description: A 60-second lesson on Anchoring Bias: The First Number Wins.

hook.text: A jacket 'was' $200, now $99. The $200 makes $99 feel like a steal. But what if it was always worth $99?

buildup.text: Anchoring bias: the first piece of information (the anchor) disproportionately influences subsequent judgments.

discovery.text: Pricing pages show the expensive plan first. The mid-tier suddenly looks reasonable by comparison.

twist.text: Anchoring Bias has a twist: the obvious interpretation usually breaks down.

climax.text: Apple announces iPhone at $999. Then shows the 'affordable' model at $699. $699 feels cheap — because of the anchor.

punchline.text: You don't evaluate prices in a vacuum.

quiz.question: How does anchoring bias affect pricing perception?
options: The first price seen becomes a reference point that makes later prices seem cheaper
People always choose the cheapest option
Higher prices make people leave the page

details.summary: Anchoring bias means the first piece of information encountered heavily influences subsequent judgments. In design, showing a high original price before the sale price makes the discount feel larger. The anchor doesn't need to be relevant — any initial number shifts perception.
details.whyItMatters: Anchoring explains why pricing pages show expensive plans first and why 'was $199, now $49' feels like a better deal than simply '$49.' Understanding this bias lets designers frame information to influence perception ethically.
takeaways: The first number encountered anchors all subsequent judgments
Original prices make discounts feel larger than standalone prices
Anchors work even when they are arbitrary or irrelevant

faq.question: How do pricing pages use anchoring?
faq.answer: Many SaaS pricing pages show the most expensive enterprise plan first, making the mid-tier plan seem reasonable by comparison. Showing 'was $299' crossed out next to '$99' creates an anchor that makes $99 feel like a bargain. Without the anchor, $99 is evaluated on its own merits.

faq.question: Can you overcome anchoring bias?
faq.answer: Awareness helps but doesn't eliminate it — anchoring persists even when people know about it. Counter-strategies include seeking multiple independent reference points, delaying judgment until more information is available.
